facts.fact: The F-35C is a single-seat, single-engine strike fighter that operates from conventional runways and aircraft carriers. The pilot and wingman therefore occupy separate aircraft, not front and rear seats in one jet.
Keep variant behavior consistent: the F-35C is the catapult-launched carrier variant with folding wingtips. Vertical landing is an F-35B capability, not an F-35C capability.

Radio and visual acknowledgement are real formation practices. Air Force formation-training guidance directs number two to acknowledge a visual signal with a head nod and to use radio to resolve confusion. It also specifies that 'visual' means positive visual contact with a formation aircraft. This supports a restrained acknowledgement beat, but is not evidence of an F-35-specific attack gesture or exact naval combat dialogue.

The F-35 has no separate physical head-up display: flight symbology and sensor imagery are projected onto the helmet visor. Six external infrared cameras provide imagery that can let the pilot see a view otherwise blocked by aircraft structure; the aircraft itself does not become transparent.

An F-35C attack on a ship using laser-guided weapons has a documented precedent. On August 15, 2021, F-35Cs launched from USS Carl Vinson participated in strikes against decommissioned frigate ex-USS Ingraham in the Hawaiian Islands Operating Area. The Navy account does not identify the precise bomb model, and the sinking involved multiple aircraft, ships, missiles and a submarine—not just two F-35s.

The GBU-12 Paveway II is a laser-guided bomb using a 500-pound general-purpose warhead. Laser-guided bombs detect and track a target illuminated by a laser; they should not be portrayed as independently radar-seeking anti-ship missiles.

The F-35C demonstrated GBU-12 employment against a moving land target on March 29, 2017, using an inert bomb and aircraft targeting/release logic. This verifies the aircraft–weapon pairing and a moving-target demonstration; it does not by itself establish performance against a maneuvering, defended warship.

If using the Ingraham exercise as a factual setting, depict a decommissioned target hulk, not an active enemy vessel returning fire. The Navy described environmental preparation and safeguards, with the exercise requiring at least 6,000 feet of water and a location at least 50 nautical miles from land.

story.story:
Over Meridian Range, Vega’s F-35C and Rook’s F-35C race above blue ocean, gray wings spread, twin tails canted outward. Guitar and drums punch through engine thunder.

Inside Vega’s F-35C, Vega turns a dark helmet toward Rook’s F-35C. Sunlight flashes across the broad reflective visor. A ribbed oxygen hose crosses an olive-green flight suit.

“Rook, you with me?” Vega’s radio crackles.

“Right here, Vega.”

Inside Rook’s F-35C, Rook looks across at Vega and gives one firm nod. Vega nods back.

Ahead, the gray frigate Harrow floats beneath a tall mast. A caption reads: “MERIDIAN RANGE. HARROW: DECOMMISSIONED TARGET.”

On Vega’s wide touchscreen, Harrow sits beneath a crosshair. “LASER” illuminates beside the image.

Vega’s F-35C and Rook’s F-35C bank toward Harrow. Each releases a GBU-12 Paveway II bomb from a wing pylon. The camera follows the two GBU-12 Paveway II bombs downward, narrow noses leading, rear fins spread.

Two impacts punch fire and spray along Harrow. Smoke rolls above the mast.

Vega’s F-35C and Rook’s F-35C climb together. The guitar cuts out.

Black. White lettering: “F-35C. TOGETHER, ON TARGET.”
